experiments.title: Does stroke-score 0.2 hold on text it never saw, and does it beat plain ink measures?
experiments.question: The 0.2 thresholds were set on three known-text segments, and the contrast line was added after the PHerc. 0343 check. Do they hold on new text, and is the rule better than simply measuring how much ink the models see?
experiments.technique: Thresholds frozen first: tag stroke-score-v0.2.0. Held-out text: PHerc0841 w00, the sheet next to our 0841 control (about 0.4 mm away, so different text), on a scroll none of the 9 µm models trained on; rendered from the public CT, inked with both model sets, cut into 1 cm strips like our search bands. Baselines and ranking: known-text strips and the null windings scored with the same code; the 0.2 rule against mean ink probability, ink area and their reading-blind differences, at the same number of false alarms on the nulls, and where known text lands when it is mixed into the null ranking. On the home GPUs.
experiments.result: Thresholds frozen at stroke-score-v0.2.0, then scored on PHerc. 0841 w00, the neighbouring sheet of the 0841 control: new text that no 9 µm model trained on. With Reader v2 + d9v4C the 0.2 rule flags 14 of its 15 one-centimetre strips; with the three models (ink_9um ×2 + dense_native), 6 of 15. On the null windings it flags 8 of 294 winding-depths (Reader v2 + d9v4C) and 0 of 194 (three models); every flag was checked by eye: crack streaks and bright zones that recur on the neighbouring turns. Known-text strips against nulls: AUC 0.895 and 0.968. Plain ink amounts score as high (up to 0.99) but also tell the two text-free scrolls apart (AUC 0.95), so across scrolls they measure the scan, not the text. Mixed into the null ranking, the 0.2 margin puts 3.8 of 4.7 and 7.5 of 8.5 known strips in the top 20. On the way we found a bug: isolated invalid pixels zeroed the row score of renders with many one-pixel specks.
experiments.learned: The rule holds on new text with Reader v2 + d9v4C and is weaker with the three-model set on faint text. Released as stroke-score 0.2.1: same thresholds, the speck fix, and these numbers in the README. 0.2.2 fixes 0.2.1's packaging: an old build copy in the repository could be installed instead of the fixed code.

experiments.short: Ink first over all of PHerc0175A (cloud)
experiments.title: Brute force, option 3 at scale: ink first over a whole 8.64 µm scroll
experiments.question: Can ink first, which needs no mesh, sweep a whole scroll in an evening and point at text?
experiments.technique: PHerc0175A, the clearest of the 8.64 µm eligible scans, tiled into 199 blocks of 1280³ voxels. In each block, patches cut along the sheets of the published surface prediction (one point per 0.8 mm cube), inked with Reader v2 in both layer orders, summarised per block and mapped over the scroll. Four cloud GPUs, about four hours.
experiments.result: 129,125 patches over the whole scroll, no failures, and nothing writing-like. Hot patches are about as common on the reading side as on the other (1.42 % and 1.31 %), and the hottest are saturated blobs on cracks, holes and crushed fibres. The positive control on PHerc. 343 afterwards (next entry) showed that this sampling puts too few patches on any one sheet for a small written area to stand out, so the quiet map rules out large, strongly inked areas, not a few lines of text.

images.caption: PHerc0175A from above and from the side, every ink-first patch coloured by how much of its centre Reader v2 inks on the reading side; grey = looks like damage. The hot spots are scattered through the scroll and sit on damage; no region stands out.

experiments.learned: A whole-scroll sweep takes an evening, but at one point per 0.8 mm cube it is a coarse net. Next: a sampler that takes a point on every sheet, tested first on PHerc. 343.

experiments.short: Ink first on known 8.64 µm letters (PHerc. 343)
experiments.title: Does ink first see real 8.64 µm letters? A positive control on PHerc. 343
experiments.question: Before trusting a quiet PHerc0175A: does ink first light up on letters we know are there, in the same kind of scan?
experiments.technique: One block of PHerc. 343 holding 10 of Erwin Nieuwlaar's 18 First Letters (his letter boxes placed in 3D through his published mesh), cut and inked exactly like the PHerc0175A sweep (Reader v2 and d9v4C); every patch mapped back onto his segment.
experiments.result: Yes where it lands, and with a denser sampler it now lands. In the first run only 13 of the block's 766 patches landed on his letters: one point per 0.8 mm cube is spread over many sheets. A sampler that takes a point on every sheet piece in each cube found 4,441 patches in the same block, 69 of them on his letters. Patches on letters light up on the reading side (16 % hot with Reader v2 and with d9v4C, against 1 % of the patches elsewhere in the block) and match the mesh pipeline's map of the same spots (r 0.61). About a quarter of all hot reading-side patches sit on his letters, which hold under 2 % of the patches: some 15 times more than chance. The block as a whole stands out less: 1.2 % of its patches are hot on the reading side against 0.8–0.9 % on the other side, where one cluster of hot patches is as big as the letters' (27–35 patches).

images.caption: Nieuwlaar's PHerc. 343 segment in reading orientation. Grey: our Reader v2 map from the mesh pipeline, with his letters inside the boxes. Squares: ink-first patch centres (1.1 mm), coloured by how much they ink, filled when hot. Top: reading side; bottom: the other side. Most letters get no patch at all.

experiments.learned: With a point on every sheet, ink first finds 8.64 µm letters at about 15 times chance. A second sweep has to rank clusters of hot patches against the other side's, not whole blocks: block totals barely move.

experiments.short: Is the ink in the raw CT?
experiments.title: Is there an ink signal in the raw CT itself, without a model?
experiments.question: The CT shows the papyrus weave, cracks and holes in fine detail but never the ink. Is the ink in the data at all at 8.64 µm, and can we see it without a model?
experiments.technique: On Nieuwlaar's PHerc. 343 segment: the CT brightness along the normal inside the letter strokes against the papyrus between them; the same split by where the surface sits inside a voxel; plain-CT images made to bring out a brighter written face.
experiments.result: On PHerc. 343 the CT inside the strokes is about 8 units brighter (about 6 % of the scan's range) through the written sheet, peaking two voxels in; where the surface sits inside a voxel matters a little (about 15 % weaker contrast in the worst quarter). But the strokes there were picked by the ink models, which may favour bright spots. A check on PHerc. 0841's human-labelled letters (9.36 µm) the next day found almost no brightness difference at any depth from −12 to +12 (AUC 0.48–0.56), while the models read the same letters at AUC 0.82–0.86. Taking the papyrus weave out of the CT (a running median along the fibres, or damping the fibre directions in the Fourier spectrum) did not bring the letters out on either scroll. No plain-CT image shows the letters; the models' maps show them plainly.

images.caption: PHerc. 343, Nieuwlaar's letters (boxes) in reading orientation. Top three panels: CT only (the rendered layer; the written face, smoothed; the written face minus the gap in front). Bottom: the five-model ink map. The letters show only in the bottom panel. 1 cm bars.

experiments.learned: The ink is not simply brighter in these scans; whatever the models respond to across the 17 layers is subtler than brightness or weave. Only trained models pull it out, so understanding what they see, and better models for this kind of scan, are the levers.

experiments.title: Real letters light up in every model; false alarms in some
experiments.question: Our false alarms often show in one or two models only. Does counting how many of six independently trained models see a spot one-sided separate letters from damage?
experiments.technique: Six models (Nieuwlaar's four, Reader v2 and d9v4C) on PHerc. 343 at the letters' depth, and our six-model deep look at PHerc0813 w079 (a spot Ted picked in the viewer): per tile, how many models see the reading side brighter than the blind side by more than a fifth of their own spread.
experiments.result: At least five of the six agree on 78 % of 343's 18 letters, on 10 % of 39 tiles of its bare papyrus, and on 25 % of the w079 spot's 8 tiles; there, only the two models that flagged it saw a one-sided signal, and no model shows strokes. On clean 9.36 µm papyrus (six crops, three windings each of PHerc0813 and PHerc0191, depths 0 to +2) five or more agree on 2 of 129 tiles (1.6 %), both on one PHerc0813 winding. The full deep look at w079 (six models, depths −15 to +15) is done: no letter strokes at any depth.
experiments.learned: Agreement separates 343's letters from its bare papyrus and from the crack-and-hole false alarms, and it almost never fires on clean 9.36 µm papyrus. Still to check: how often it fires on known 9.36 µm text (PHerc0841).

experiments.short: Do false alarms sit on damage?
experiments.title: Damage maps, flat and in 3D: our false alarms are not on damaged papyrus
experiments.question: Many of our false alarms looked like they sat on cracks, holes and torn edges. If they do, a damage map would let us search the clean papyrus first and set aside flags that fall on damage.
experiments.technique: Flat (2D): per 1.5 mm tile of each 66-layer render, the share of holes, cracks (thin dark lines at least 0.3 mm long), distance to the mesh edge, sheet wander and brightness, next to the ink the way stroke-score sees it, on PHerc. 343 (letter boxes), PHerc0841 (human labels) and 150 null windings of PHerc0813 and PHerc0191; two versions of the hole rule. In 3D: the structure of the CT around the PHerc0813 z12000 band (how sheet-like and how ordered the layers are, dark gaps, cracks that cut across sheets), sampled along each mesh node's own normal 1.5 mm in front of and behind the sheet, so that a crack running through several turns counts.
experiments.result: On the null windings the hottest tiles are no more damaged than the rest (AUC 0.47–0.59 on every measure, about chance), and the eight flags we had already judged false alarms sit at the 37th–55th percentile of their winding: ordinary papyrus by this map. Masking out the damage removes half the area and moves the hot rate only from 4.7 % to 4.6 %. In 3D the answer is the same and, if anything, the other way round: hot tiles sit on flatter, better ordered, slightly less cracked papyrus than the rest, and cross-sections under the flags show stacked, orderly sheets.

images.caption: PHerc0813 w079 in reading orientation with the 2D damage map: holes red, cracks yellow, and the top 5 % of reading-side stroke tiles outlined in cyan. Most of the hottest tiles sit on plain papyrus, away from the holes and cracks. 5 mm bar.

experiments.learned: Damage does not explain our false alarms, so a damage mask would not remove them. What makes a clean-looking spot light up is something about the papyrus itself, which is what the ablation and agreement tests now ask.

experiments.title: An 8.64 µm ink model from PHerc. 343, first try: it memorised its letters
experiments.question: Most public ink models were trained on other scans. Would a model fine-tuned on 8.64 µm text see 8.64 µm ink better? The only labelled native 8.64 µm text we have is Erwin Nieuwlaar's PHerc. 343 segment.
experiments.technique: dense_native fine-tuned on his segment for 3,000 steps at home (about an hour; villa's ink training). Labels: the top 20 % of our five-model ensemble inside his letter boxes. Letters 1–6 held out, the rest for training. Compared with dense_native as it is: AUC on the held-out and the training letters, and how much clean 9.36 µm papyrus and the PHerc0813 w079 false alarm read as ink.
experiments.result: Worse on the letters it had not seen: AUC 0.989 for dense_native, 0.959 for the best checkpoint, 0.933 for the last. Better on the letters it trained on (0.970 → 0.992 → 0.999). More clean papyrus read as ink: 0.03–4.9 % → 2.4–10 % → 6–13.5 %.

images.caption: The six held-out PHerc. 343 letters (boxes, after Nieuwlaar), reading side at d +1. Top: dense_native as published. Middle and bottom: our fine-tune, best and last checkpoint. The fine-tune is sharper but lights up more papyrus outside the letters.

experiments.learned: Twelve letters labelled by our own ensemble teach a model to copy the ensemble on those letters, not to see ink. A better 8.64 µm model needs real labels: strokes traced by people, from published sources. Until then dense_native as it is stays in the pipeline.

experiments.title: Housekeeping: the code sorted into what works, what is being tested and what didn't work
experiments.question: After six days the scripts had grown into one folder of 130, where a dead end sat next to the step every search depends on. Can someone new tell which is which at a glance?
experiments.technique: Every script moved into one of pipeline/ (checked on known text, used for every search), experiments/ (being tested; a STATUS.md with the question, the numbers so far and what decides it), dead-ends/ (a README with what we tried, the numbers and why it failed), archive/ (one-off or replaced, with what replaced it) and infra/ (plumbing). The run scripts went with the idea they tested. Only moves and path fixes; the machine that runs the jobs keeps a flat script folder, and a small sync script maps the two by file name.
experiments.result: 223 files moved, each listed old → new in infra/moved-2026-10-13.tsv; nine dead ends written up; the code dictionary regrouped the same way. The released stroke-score keeps its install path.
experiments.learned: A dead end that is written down is a result. Kept apart from the pipeline, it stops anyone, us included, from picking it up again by accident.

experiments.title: Brute force, band 2 on PHerc0813: z 8,000–10,500, searched and blank
experiments.question: Does the tall-band recipe keep working one band further down PHerc0813, and is there writing there?
experiments.technique: The same exp-30k spiral fit on z 8,000–10,500, snap, Lasagna flatten, 66-layer render, Reader v2 + d9v4C at depths 0 and +1 on all 76 windings (152 winding-depths), scored with stroke-score 0.2 and the flags checked by eye.
experiments.result: Three flags (w047 at d 0, w088 at d 0 and +1), all false alarms. w047 shows the same diffuse speckle on both faces of the sheet (the brightest blob is on the other face); its rows come from a crushed, folded lower half whose layers run in long parallel bands. w088 is speckle on both faces with a bright streak along the mesh edge and a vertical band. With the band above, our PHerc0813 search now covers 210 windings over 75–122 mm of the scroll's height.

images.caption: PHerc0813: where we have looked. Every fitted winding where it crosses a CT slice, from above and from the side. Blue: rendered, inked, scored, nothing found; orange: flagged by stroke-score 0.2 and checked by eye, not text. 210 windings in three bands, 75–122 mm.

experiments.learned: The tall-band recipe tiles PHerc0813 band after band. Both new bands are blank, and every flag was damage or geometry: folds, cracks, strip and mesh edges. PHerc0813 stops here for now; it is crowded with other teams.

experiments.title: Held out, part 2: the frozen 0.2 rule on 304 blank winding-depths it never saw
experiments.question: We froze stroke-score's thresholds at the tag stroke-score-v0.2.0 and tested them on new text (PHerc0841 w00). Do they also keep their false-alarm rate on new blank papyrus?
experiments.technique: The two PHerc0813 bands searched after the freeze (z 8,000–10,500 and 10,500–13,000; 152 winding-depths each, Reader v2 + d9v4C at d 0 and +1), scored with the frozen rule; every flag checked by eye.
experiments.result: 6 of 304 winding-depths flagged (2.0 %), against 2.7 % on the 294 null winding-depths the rule was set on. None of the six is writing: blobs along cracks and strip edges, the bands of a fold, a streak along a mesh edge. The write-up of stroke-score 0.2 with both held-out tests is on its own page (stroke-score-0.2.html), and it went in for the October Progress Prize.
experiments.learned: The false-alarm rate held on new blank papyrus, and the flags it raises are the known kinds. The rule is a triage line, not a detector: every flag still needs a look next to the CT.

experiments.short: Our whole pipeline finds the 343 letters
experiments.title: End to end on PHerc. 343: our own geometry and read put all 18 of Erwin Nieuwlaar's letters where they should be
experiments.question: Our controls so far started from other people's meshes. If we run our whole recipe from scratch on a scroll with known letters, do the letters land on our windings and show in our read?
experiments.technique: In the cloud: our centre (VC3D vc_gen_umbilicus + smoothing), sheet tracks with the organisers' PHerc0813 parameters, the exp-30k spiral fit on z 9,300–11,300 of PHerc. 343 (8.64 µm), Nieuwlaar's snap (120 windings, 94 % of mesh points on the sheet), Lasagna flatten. Then Nieuwlaar's 18 letters, placed in 3D from his published segment, matched to our windings (within 4 voxels along the normal), and our read of those windings with Reader v2 + d9v4C at d 0 and +1, letter areas against the rest of the winding.
experiments.result: All 18 letters lie on four of our windings (w047–w050), a median 0.7 voxel from our surface. On our read they show as rows of strokes on the reading side. Letters against the rest of the winding: AUC 0.78 (Reader v2) and 0.74 (d9v4C) on w047, 0.73 and 0.71 on w048, 0.62–0.63 on w049 and 0.52–0.57 on w050 (few, faint letters); the other face lower (0.65–0.72 on w047–w048). Neither model was trained on PHerc0343 (Reader v2 and d9v4C trained on PHerc0343P, a separately scanned object).

images.caption: PHerc. 343, our winding w047, Reader v2 + d9v4C at d 0. Left: the reading side and the other face; right: the same with the areas of Erwin Nieuwlaar's letters outlined. The letters sit where our read shows strokes.

experiments.learned: The whole chain works on known text: our own centre, tracks, fit, snap and flatten reach the inked sheet, and our read shows the letters. Our blank results elsewhere are not a geometry failure in disguise.

experiments.short: Six-model agreement on hot blank crops
experiments.title: Six models agreeing is a supporting check, not a test: it also scores high on the hottest blank crops
experiments.question: On clean blank papyrus five or six of our models almost never agree on one face (1.6 % of tiles) while on known letters they do (78 %). Does that hold on the hottest crops of our blank bands, the places a search would look at first?
experiments.technique: The six models (ink_9um ×2, dense_native, Hecate, Reader v2, d9v4C) at d 0 and +1 on crops around the top-ranked spot of the 15 best windings of the PHerc0813 tall band and of PHerc0191 z11200; the share of 2.8 mm tiles where at least 5 of 6 are one-sided. Also the official ink labels of PHerc0841 ag144 and PHerc0139 w030/w045, with models trained on them left out.
experiments.result: On the hot blank crops, 38–40 % of tiles (PHerc0813; w072 88 %, w071 71 %) and 21 % (PHerc0191) have five or six models agreeing. By eye PHerc0813 w072 is soft one-sided blobs along a crack, with no rows and no stroke shapes. On the official labels, letter tiles agree 83–100 %, but background tiles 30–46 %.

images.caption: PHerc0813 w072, the hot blank crop where 88 % of tiles had five or six models agreeing: the CT, the reading side (four-model mean) and the other face, in reading orientation. Soft blobs along a crack, not rows of strokes. 1 cm bar.

experiments.learned: The models agree on whatever lights them up, including crack zones, so agreement cannot tell text from the hottest blank crops. Use it to back up rows, stroke shapes and depth, not instead of them.

experiments.short: A machine letter reader on 9 µm maps
experiments.title: A Greek letter reader on our 9 µm ink maps of known text: not yet
experiments.question: Chase Hendrick published a small line reader that names Greek capitals on ink maps, with its own scrambled-copy controls. Can it read known letters on our 9 µm maps, as a first machine check before human readers?
experiments.technique: Run locally on CPU (letters-v2-real weights, checked by sha256) on our maps of known text: PHerc. 343 w047 and w048 (14–15 of Nieuwlaar's letters each; Reader v2 + d9v4C, d 0 and +1) and PHerc0841 ag144 (official labels; five models), in four orientations, with the letter height measured from the known letters and estimated by the reader; the other face as a control.
experiments.result: It kept 1–5 letters on windings with 14–15 known letters, about as many as on its own scrambled copies, and as many on the other face of the sheet; 0–3 on PHerc0841. Its letter-height estimate fell back to a default on our maps.

images.caption: The reader on our PHerc. 343 w048 map (render orientation): it names four letters (Ω, Φ, Ι, Δ) among the roughly 15 there. Model output, not a reading.

experiments.learned: The reader is shown to work on 2.4 µm maps; our 9 µm maps are softer and it does not read them yet, as its author says. It would need training on 9 µm maps of transcribed text.

experiments.short: Ink first on PHerc0841's labelled text
experiments.title: Ink first, with a point on every sheet, on two labelled PHerc0841 blocks: one passes, one does not
experiments.question: Ink first reads 3D blocks without meshes. On known 9.36 µm text with human labels, do the patches on the letters light up more than the rest of the block?
experiments.technique: Two 1,280³ blocks around PHerc0841's labelled segments ag2814 and w00; sheet-like points from the surface prediction (about 5,000 per block), a 256-voxel patch at each, Reader v2 and d9v4C both ways; patches on letters against patches on the segment outside the letters and elsewhere in the block.
experiments.result: ag2814: on the letters the d9v4C hot fraction is 0.20 against 0.09 elsewhere in the block (2.3×). w00: 0.05 on the letters against 0.09 elsewhere: no signal.
experiments.learned: Ink first can find labelled text, but not reliably: on one of two segments it misses. It stays a tool for picking places to look, behind the mesh pipeline.

experiments.short: Five ideas of our own, on known text first
experiments.title: Five ideas of our own for seeing ink better, each tested on known text first: none passed
experiments.question: Before any new idea touches an unread scroll, does it help on letters we already know: PHerc. 343 (Erwin Nieuwlaar's labels) and the labelled PHerc0841 segments?
experiments.technique: Every idea got its pass line written down before it ran, and was tuned on one half of the known text and judged on the other half. (1) An ink signature in the raw CT: band-pass texture and brightness per layer and scale, with a logistic readout. (2) The thickness of the surface coating along the normal. (3) How letter-like the marks' shapes are: stroke width, elongation, branches, row spacing, trained on one set of sources and tested on another. (4) Ridge filters (Frangi, Sato, Meijering) on the ink maps. (5) Deconvolution of the maps with a blur kernel learned from the labels (a Wiener filter).
experiments.result: Raw-CT ink signature: held-out AUC 0.51–0.67 against a pass line of 0.75. Coating thickness: AUC 0.52, no difference between ink and papyrus. Letter-likeness: AUC 0.68 and 0.74 across sources, against 0.8 both ways. Ridge filters: Dice ×0.97–1.00 and AUC −0.001 to −0.008 on 343 and 0841. Deconvolution: a small gain on 0841 (Dice ×1.03–1.05, AUC +0.008 to +0.022), short of the ×1.10 bar, and the same setting cost 3 % Dice on 343. The setting that won was the mildest, which is mostly smoothing along the learned kernel. That kernel is about 0.3 mm across.
experiments.learned: On known text the plain ink map is as good as anything we could do to it afterwards. A filter can smooth away noise, but it cannot add stroke detail the map does not carry. Better letters have to come from what goes into the map: the models and the geometry.

experiments.short: How much letter detail a 9 µm ink map carries
experiments.title: A ruler for legibility against the 2.4 µm truth: our 9 µm maps agree at the scale of whole letters, not strokes
experiments.question: Every sharpening idea scored "same as the plain map" on PHerc. 343. But 343's labels are outlines of whole letters and the plain map already matches them, so that test cannot see sharper strokes. Can a ruler that compares against a high-resolution truth tell what a 9 µm ink map really holds?
experiments.technique: Known text with a 2.4 µm truth, held out from the models we compared: PHerc0841 w00 and auto_grown 20260221022814 (human ink labels drawn on the 2.4 µm scan, and the organisers' 2.4 µm ink prediction), and PHerc0139 w047 (the 2.4 µm / 78 keV prediction; dense_native and ink_9um only, since d9v4C trained on it). Our maps at depth +1 against the truth downsampled onto the 9 µm grid, with three measures: Fourier ring correlation by spatial period, Pearson r, and the contrast between labelled strokes and the 0.05–0.3 mm around them. Intervals come from resampling tiles. Gates were written before each run: the ruler had to react to added noise and to blur before it could be used.
experiments.result: Both versions of the ruler, first on the stroke band (periods 0.2–1 mm), then on the letter band (0.5–2.4 mm), failed their own gates, and that is the finding. Below about 0.4 mm nothing correlates with the 2.4 µm truth, not even the 2.4 µm human labels with the 2.4 µm prediction: the ring correlation is near 0 there, against 0.43–0.47 at 0.8 mm. Blurring our maps by 0.1 mm, or even 0.3 mm, does not lower their match to the truth, so the detail they carry is coarser than about 0.25 mm. Down to about 0.5 mm our maps match the 2.4 µm prediction about as well as the human labels do on one PHerc0841 segment, and somewhat less well on the other. The model ranking was the same in every run. On PHerc0841, Reader v2 and d9v4C match best (r 0.69–0.77), then dense_native (0.63–0.67), then the two ink_9um seeds (0.47–0.62). On PHerc0139 w047, dense_native 0.58 against 0.38–0.40 for the seeds. Display filters (median, unsharp mask) did not change the match. We stopped after two versions on purpose: a third ruler, tuned after two looks at the data, would be fitted to the answer.

images.caption: PHerc0841 w00, the same 5 mm crop: the organisers' 2.4 µm ink prediction (top left) and our 9 µm maps (five-model mean, the ink_9um seeds as one vote, and without them). The 2.4 µm map shows a ring-shaped letter where the 9 µm maps show blobs. 1 mm bar.

experiments.learned: At 9 µm these models carry letter-scale information but no stroke detail we can check. Gains in legibility have to come from better models and better geometry, and the honest ruler for legibility is people reading blind tiles with known letters mixed in.

experiments.short: A peak at the surface is not evidence of ink
experiments.title: On blank papyrus the strongest model marks also peak at the surface; the difference is that the other face sees them too
experiments.question: On known letters the ink models' marks peak sharply at the sheet surface and fade within about ±10 layers. Is that depth curve evidence of ink?
experiments.technique: The same depth profile on PHerc. 343's labelled letters and on two windings of PHerc0191 and PHerc0813 where our searches found no writing: marks picked in one model's map at the surface, then scored in another model's map at every depth from −15 to +15, on both faces (AUC of the marks against the rest).
experiments.result: On the blank windings the marks also peak at depth 0, with AUC 0.98–0.99, so the shape of the curve says nothing about ink. The other face at the peak differs more often than not: 0.80–0.92 for three of the four model and winding pairs on blank papyrus, where the marks show from both faces, but 0.64 for the fourth (d9v4C on the PHerc0191 winding), inside the 0.63–0.66 of 343's one-sided letters.
experiments.learned: The depth curve is no evidence of ink. One-sidedness separates ink from blank papyrus in most cases but not all, so it is a hint to weigh, not a rule; it needs many more blank windings first.

experiments.short: What each ink model was trained on
experiments.title: What each ink model we use was trained on, from the model cards and configs
experiments.question: Which known-text segments are honest tests for which ink models, and which are their training data?
experiments.technique: For Reader v2, d9v4C, dense_native, the ink_9um seeds 42 and 43 and Hecate: the model cards, training configs, label manifests and published checksums. The checkpoints we run match the published hashes where there are any.
experiments.result: Of the eligible scrolls we have searched, none appears in the five published training lists. PHerc0841 is held out by design for Reader v2 and d9v4C. Paris 4 is training data for every one of these models, so a Paris 4 check tests a pipeline, not a model. dense_native and ink_9um were not trained on PHerc. 343, so 343 is an independent test for them. Reader v2 and d9v4C trained on PHerc0343P, a separate scan made the same day with the same settings. There's a naming trap: the ink_9um label set calls PHerc0139 segments w016, w017, w028 and w029, which are the public w029, w030, w044 and w045. So w030 and w045 are training data for ink_9um, dense_native and Reader v2. d9v4C was trained on PHerc0139 w047, and also on w024, w048, w053 and the title. Hecate's training list is not published, and the bucket it was developed on holds PHerc0841's labels, so treat 0841 as seen by Hecate.
experiments.learned: Look a segment up here before scoring any model on it. Our own earlier credits table had w030 and w045 marked clean, which was wrong.

experiments.short: Earlier ink_9um checkpoints, and an ensemble of them
experiments.title: Earlier ink_9um checkpoints, and an average of all of them, read known text only slightly better than the last one
experiments.question: The ink_9um hybrid models (seeds 42 and 43) are published every 10k steps up to 75k, and we had been running the last step. Do earlier steps, or an ensemble of several, read held-out text more clearly?
experiments.technique: All published steps of both seeds (10k to 75k) and each seed's average of them, at depth +1, on two held-out PHerc0841 segments with the official human ink labels (w00 and auto_grown 20260221022814), and on two windings where no writing was found (PHerc0191 w060, PHerc0813 w102) for false alarms. A combination is chosen on one 0841 segment and judged on the other, both ways. Pass line, fixed before the run: Dice at least 1.10 times the plain pair (both seeds at 75k) and AUC no lower than the plain pair's minus 0.005, both ways, with false alarms no higher than the larger of 1.2 times plain and plain plus 0.01.
experiments.result: Fail. The best combination, both seeds at all seven steps, raised Dice only 1.08 and 1.03 times (0.548 against 0.507, 0.578 against 0.559), with AUC 0.774 against 0.762 and 0.800 against 0.798; false alarms stayed at the plain pair's level. On the same segments Reader v2 reaches Dice 0.59 and 0.63 and AUC 0.82 and 0.85.
experiments.learned: Averaging the published ink_9um steps is a small gain at best. Reader v2 stays the stronger reader on held-out 9 µm text.

experiments.short: A short fine-tune of Reader v2 on one labelled segment
experiments.title: A short fine-tune of Reader v2 on one labelled segment makes it worse everywhere else, with either optimizer
experiments.question: Can Reader v2 learn from a handful of new human labels without losing what it already reads? We tested the recipe on official labels of a scroll it never saw.
experiments.technique: Reader v2 (step 40000) fine-tuned with villa's flat ink training on the official human labels of PHerc0841 w00 (dense: 23 % of the checked area is ink), 1,000 steps, checkpoints every 250, with two recipes: AdamW at 1e-5 with BCE plus Dice, and SGD (Nesterov, momentum 0.99, as in Reader v2's own training) at 1e-3 with BCE only. Judged on the neighbouring 0841 sheet auto_grown 20260221022814 (different text, never trained on), on PHerc. 343 (Erwin Nieuwlaar's letters), and on six blank crops from windings with no writing, by the share of the window read at 0.5 or more. Pass lines, written before the run: the unseen sheet's AUC at least Reader v2's minus 0.01, 343 at least minus 0.02, blank papyrus no more than 0.5 points above Reader v2 and no crop above 2 %.
experiments.result: Both recipes fail, already after 250 steps. The segment it trained on gets better (AUC 0.86 to 0.92-0.93), while the unseen sheet drops (0.818 to 0.787), 343 drops (0.981 to 0.93-0.94) and blank papyrus read as ink rises from 0.3 % to 17-19 % (24-27 % by step 1,000). The optimizer makes no difference. The model has no running normalisation statistics, so this is not a statistics drift.
experiments.learned: Fine-tuning a model trained on many scrolls with one segment over-fits it to that segment and costs it everywhere else. New labels need to be mixed with labelled data from many scrolls in every batch, the way Reader v2 itself was trained, or added in far smaller steps.

experiments.short: A letter guesser on known 9 µm text
experiments.title: A "which letter could this blob be" guesser does no better than always guessing the commonest letters
experiments.question: Could a guesser that fits letter outlines to the marks on a 9 µm ink map at least point a reader to the right letters, as a search aid?
experiments.technique: We named 22 letters by eye on three held-out PHerc0841 crops against the official ink labels (no ink model saw 0841). The guesser places a guess where Reader v2 marks a letter-sized area and ranks the 24 Greek letters by how well their outlines fit the marks there. Pass line, fixed before scoring: the true letter in the top 3 at 9 or more letters, and better than the same guesser on tile-shuffled windows (p < 0.05).
experiments.result: Fail. Only 10 of the 22 letters got a guess at all (Reader v2 covers parts of letters, not whole ones). Of those 10 the true letter was in the top 3 three times; always guessing alpha, epsilon and omicron gets 6, the shuffled windows 2 (p = 0.15).
experiments.learned: At 9 µm the maps do not carry enough letter shape for a shape guesser to beat letter frequencies. We shelved it; a reader fitting outlines by hand stays a human job.

experiments.title: Simple rules that should throw out false marks do not separate real letters from marks on blank papyrus
experiments.question: The ink models also mark blank papyrus. Can cheap per-mark rules (each one weak) throw out most of those false marks while keeping real letters, the way computer-aided detection in medicine filters its candidates?
experiments.technique: Marks: Reader v2's strong marks at depth +1 (contrast to a 3 mm local mean). Known letters: marks centred on the official labels of three held-out PHerc0841 sheets (27 letter marks) and on Erwin Nieuwlaar's PHerc. 343 letters. Blank hits: 847 marks on windings of PHerc0813 and 0191 where no writing was found. Rules: one-sidedness, agreement with a second model, fibre direction, along-fibre shape, CT density, distance to the surface's edge, a line-grid layout, crackle, and whether a mark repeats on the neighbouring turn. Pass line per rule, fixed first: keep 90 % of the 0841 letter marks and remove at least 30 % of the blank hits.
experiments.result: Fail for every rule: they remove 0 to 23 % of the blank hits. Two early passes on only 12 letter marks did not hold with 27. Agreement with a second model looked like a pass (66 %) but every mark on the 0841 renders scores high, letter or not: it tells the scroll apart, not ink. On the neighbouring turn the test ran the other way: letter marks repeat there more often than blank marks, because the 17-layer model window reaches the next sheet. Marks are also not concentrated at the surface edges or on stretched mesh.
experiments.learned: At 9 µm a model's strong marks on known text and on blank papyrus look alike on everything we can measure at the mark. The depth-profile rule is still running.

experiments.short: Sharpening the CT before the model reads it
experiments.title: Sharpening the CT before the model reads it does not sharpen the ink map
experiments.question: The ink maps are blurrier than the letters. If the CT that goes into the model is sharpened first, does the model draw sharper strokes?
experiments.technique: An unsharp mask on every layer of the 66-layer render (light and stronger), Reader v2 at depth +1 otherwise unchanged. Judged on the three held-out PHerc0841 sheets against the official labels, PHerc. 343 against Nieuwlaar's labels, and six blank crops of PHerc0191 and 0813. Pass line, fixed first: AUC up by at least 0.01 on two of the three 0841 sheets, down by more than 0.005 on none, and no more blank papyrus read as ink (+0.5 points at most).
experiments.result: Fail. AUC changed by +0.003, +0.003 and 0.000 (light) and +0.005, +0.006 and -0.002 (stronger); blank crops 0.25 % to 0.28 %. The CT looks crisper; the maps look the same.

images.caption: CT layer 33 (top) and Reader v2 (below), plain, light and stronger sharpening: a letter area of held-out PHerc0841 and a blank PHerc0191 crop

experiments.learned: The blur is the model's own: sharpening its output (deconvolution, 15 Oct) and now its input both leave the strokes as they were.

experiments.short: A small learned combiner of five models
experiments.title: A small learned combiner of the five public 9 µm models reads held-out text slightly worse than Reader v2 alone
experiments.question: Each public model sees ink a little differently. Can a small learner on top of their maps, which cannot memorise a sheet the way a fine-tune can, combine them into a sharper reader?
experiments.technique: Gradient-boosted trees (scikit-learn) on 31 features per pixel: the reading side, the other face and their difference for Reader v2, d9v4C, dense_native and both ink_9um seeds at depth +1, at three scales, and the five-model mean; trained on about 2 million labelled pixels of PHerc0841 (two sheets), PHerc0139 (two segments) and PHerc. 343 minus a held-out quarter. Judged on the held-out PHerc0841 sheet ag2814 with the pass line of our training test: AUC up by 0.03 and letter Dice in ten agreed letters 1.3 times Reader v2's, no harm on 343's held-out quarter or on blank crops.
experiments.result: Fail. AUC 0.802 against Reader v2's 0.815; median letter Dice 0.336 against 0.366 (some letters a little better, the hard ones still 0); 343's held-out quarter 0.997 against 0.993; blank crops read as ink 5.1 % against 0.3 %.
experiments.learned: What a combiner learns on these labelled sheets does not carry to an unseen sheet of the same scroll.

experiments.short: Teaching a 9 µm model with 2.4 µm-traced labels
experiments.title: Teaching Reader v2 with ink traced on a 2.4 µm scan improves the sheets it learns and not the one next to them
experiments.question: PHerc0841 has official ink labels drawn on its 2.4 µm scan and renders at 9.4 µm in register. If Reader v2 is taught with those labels on the 9.4 µm renders, does it read a held-out 0841 sheet more clearly?
experiments.technique: Reader v2 fine-tuned 1,500 steps (AdamW, learning rate 1e-5, villa's ink training) on two 0841 sheets with their official labels, mixed in every batch with known text of other scrolls (PHerc0139, PHerc. 343 minus a held-out quarter) and blank papyrus of PHerc0191 and 0813 so it cannot drift. Held out: the neighbouring 0841 sheet ag2814, 343's quarter, six blank crops. Pass line, fixed before training: ag2814 AUC up by 0.03 and letter Dice 1.3 times Reader v2's, no harm elsewhere; the last passing checkpoint counts.
experiments.result: Fail at every checkpoint. On the sheets it was taught, AUC rose from 0.855 to 0.924; on the held-out sheet next to them it fell from 0.818 to 0.814 (step 250) and 0.789 (step 1,500). Letter Dice never beat Reader v2. 343 and the blank crops stayed fine.
experiments.learned: With this model and recipe, teaching from 2.4 µm-traced labels learns the taught sheets rather than ink. A better base model is the lever, not more fine-tuning.

experiments.title: Averaging many marks of the same shape, as cryo-EM does with molecules, still gives blobs on known 9 µm text
experiments.question: A text repeats its letters. If the marks on an ink map are grouped by shape and each group averaged, the way cryo-EM averages thousands of noisy copies of a molecule, do letter forms appear that no single mark shows?
experiments.technique: Reference-free class averaging: every strong mark on the five-model mean (depth +1) cut as a 3.6 mm patch, aligned by shift and small rotation to 12 class averages by cross-correlation, reassigned and re-averaged for 15 rounds. Control: held-out PHerc0841 sheets w00 and ag2814, where the official labels of each class's members, aligned the same way, give the class's true average. Pass line, fixed first: ink and true averages correlate (median r at least 0.5 and 0.2 above shuffled classes), and at least three classes show distinct letter shapes.
experiments.result: Fail. Median r 0.55 and 0.58 against 0.49 and 0.43 with shuffled classes; by eye the class averages are central blobs and bars, with no letter form, even on known text.

images.caption: Class averages on held-out PHerc0841 ag2814: ink average, true (label) average, three members per class

experiments.learned: At 9 µm the maps break letters into blobs, and patches centred on blobs group by blob layout, not by letter.

findings.title: The ink detector is not the problem
findings.text: Calibrated on known text: three legible Greek lines, the PHerc. 343 control passes with the ensemble, and at 9.36 µm our render and ink steps reproduce the published AUCs on PHerc0139 and PHerc0841 (run 7). The early PHerc0191 nulls were geometry; since the snap + flatten the windings have clean papyrus weave. What limits our nulls now is the triage rule that decides where we look, not the detector (see below).

findings.title: Positive control passes only with the ensemble
findings.text: On the PHerc. 343 winning segment our four-model ensemble shows the letter rows; ink_9um seed 42 alone at whole-segment scale does not. Searches on 0191 need the ensemble (Hecate is the strongest single model).

findings.title: Minimal-route spiral fits sit on the sheet ~46–49% of the time
findings.text: Satisfaction = within 6 voxels and 0.45 winding of the track's sheet. Weights don't help; 3× steps gives +3 points.

findings.title: The fitted spiral never reaches the outer third
findings.text: Per-sector audit: outermost winding 3–8 mm short of the boundary in the fat sectors; initial spacing fixes the radial extent; stretching hurts the inner tracks.

findings.title: Crushed scroll = same winding count, 2.5× spacing variation by sector
findings.text: 0.13 mm on the flattened sides (ray audit under-counts there) to 0.26 mm at the ends. Needs anisotropic deformation or local spacing supervision.

findings.title: Patch growing needs its normal grids
findings.text: Without normal_grid_path the tracer produces data-independent discs. With them it partly follows sheets.

findings.title: #1 libvolcomp not installed by the VC3D build (merged upstream, villa #2008)
findings.text: One-line CMake install fix; merged on 2026-10-12.

findings.title: #2–#5 image tags, lockfile rewrite, remote-fetch aborts
findings.text: :stable tag missing; uv.lock rewritten by sync; infer and renderer abort on a single transient remote chunk fetch. Since then upstream: vc_render_tifxyz takes a remote URL as --volume (villa #1863), and a retry for inference is open as villa #1919 (not ours).

findings.title: #6 Shipped track-crossing cache rejected after download (in review, villa #2020)
findings.text: Signature uses nanosecond mtime; any download zeroes sub-second mtime. 2.4 GB downloaded for nothing; every run rebuilds. After review the fix covers all three checks, and it still catches a local edit within the same second (my first version did not; a test caught it).

findings.title: #7 Outer-shell loss silently zero for sparse shells (villa #2021, awaiting review)
findings.text: Confidence normalized by an edge spike → 0.22 < 0.25 → no valid samples, no warning. Reproduced outside the fitter.

findings.title: #8 Fiber inference needs lasagna on PYTHONPATH (merged upstream, villa #2019)
findings.text: geometry.py imports lasagna.omezarr_pyramid unguarded; the models extra does not ship it.

findings.title: The PHerc. 343 First Letters win (2026-10-08) used our pipeline plus three steps we lacked
findings.text: Spiral fit with the surface-prediction distance field, no shell, 30k steps; post-hoc snap of every vertex onto the nearest predicted sheet (±15 vox); 66-layer render swept over 31 depths through a four-model ink ensemble. All open source; adopted.

findings.title: PHerc0191: no letters where we looked
findings.text: Band z 9,000–10,000: all 99 flattened windings at depths 0 and +1 (7 four-model, 92 three-model). The community's 10 windings. The seven best clear-band windings at depths −2..+3 with four models. Phase A4 on the other 93: 60 rows over the v0.1 flag line, 25 checked by eye, none writing. But we looked closely only where the v0.1 rule flagged, and that rule misses text on an unseen scroll, so these nulls are weaker than we thought. The clear band is being re-checked with Reader v2 + d9v4C and a row score.

findings.title: Our old band was a below-average part of the scan
findings.text: Scan-Quality-Map: 0.37–0.40 for z 9,000–10,000 against a scroll median of 0.41 and 0.54 for the clearest band, where our fit is also our best (0.519 on-sheet).

findings.title: Cracks and recurring zones can look like a signal
findings.text: The strongest PHerc0191 scores (w073 and w074 at depth +2) came from soft blobs along a CT crack band, present at several depths and faintly on the blind side. The strongest PHerc0813 score (w088 with Reader v2 + d9v4C) comes from a bright zone that sits at about the same place on the neighbouring turns w086–w090, as w073–w079 do on PHerc0191; writing does not repeat turn after turn. Neither is writing.

findings.title: Next scroll: PHerc0813
findings.text: Top three at 9.362 µm on two clarity measures, round cross-section, the longest clear stretch, every input published, same orientation as PHerc0191. Then PHerc0358, then PHerc0175A.

findings.title: PHerc0813's geometry passes the Gate B bar
findings.text: Band z 12,000–13,000 with the same recipe as PHerc0191: 0.557 of track points on the sheet and 0.182 of tracks satisfied (0191's clear band: 0.519 / 0.138), the best fit numbers of the campaign. In the CT, w085–w112 (10.5–14.8 cm) show weave over most of their length: more clean papyrus per winding than 0191's best picks, which share a crushed zone. The first eight picks, inked at depths 0 and +1 with three models and with Reader v2 + d9v4C, show no writing; w088's strong score comes from a zone that recurs on the neighbouring turns.

findings.title: Our reading side is the written face
findings.text: On the PHerc. 0343 control, PHerc0191 w073 and PHerc0813 w088 the render's +layer direction points outward and the mesh lies on the inner face of the sheet, the face that carries the 0343 letters. Our reading/blind assignment matches the control; the nulls are not a swapped-side artefact.

findings.title: The method sees ink at 9.36 µm, but the v0.1 flag rule misses text on an unseen scroll
findings.text: Cloud run 7, on two known-text segments scanned at the resolution we search. Our render + ink reproduces the published AUCs (PHerc0139 w047: dense_native 0.859, Reader v2 0.860; PHerc0841: Reader v2 + d9v4C 0.83). On PHerc0139 the stroke score sees the text as it saw the PHerc. 0343 letters (reading − blind +0.019 to +0.024, best 4 cm² window 0.054–0.067 against 0.016–0.019 on the blind side). On PHerc0841, a scroll none of the models trained on, the letters show by eye as rows of letter-shaped strokes, yet reading − blind is only +0.001 to +0.009 and the window 1.0–1.4× the blind side: the v0.1 rule would not have singled it out. So windings that stayed under the line could hold text. Known text here shows as rows of elongated strokes; a row score (2.7–4.2 on known text, at most 1.47 on our windings so far) and Reader v2 + d9v4C are now part of the search.

findings.title: Upstream removed the inputs the winner used (Spiral simplification, 2026-09-23)
findings.text: surf-SDT support and the 'phase' dense-spacing mode were deleted from spiral-fitting three weeks before they won a prize. We run the pre-removal commit in a worktree to reproduce the route.

findings.title: #9 Resident-pool sidecars reused after the source store is rebuilt
findings.text: The fitter silently trained on a stale SDT pool (1 of 1,456 bricks) after the store was rebuilt at the same path. Still the case on main; waiting for villa #1883, which changes the same code, before sending a fix.

findings.title: #10 Raw spiral windings render 16–22 % too small (in review, villa #2056)
findings.text: Meshes declare a 20-voxel grid, but on our current PHerc0813 and PHerc0191 fits the nodes are 23–26 voxels apart (26–30 on an earlier fit), so unflattened renders come out 16–22 % small and the recorded areas 34–43 % low; flattened meshes are right. Fix in review as villa #2056: write the measured spacing as the scale and the area in 3D.

findings.title: stroke-score 0.1: triage for ink searches (MIT)
findings.text: Ranks windings, depths and 4 cm² windows by stroke-shaped ink on the reading side against the blind side, with review crops. Calibrated on the PHerc. 343 control and 109 null windings. stroke-score 0.2 (in progress) adds a row score calibrated at search-band height, a stroke-shape score, a neighbour-recurrence check and a known-text control kit.

findings.title: Calibrate on known text cut to your band height
findings.text: Our search bands are about 1 cm tall, so a winding shows at most two lines of text. Known text scored over a whole segment looks far stronger than it would in a band like ours; cut into 1 cm strips, it lands much closer to our null windings. stroke-score's control kit now scores known text at any band height (--band-mm).

findings.title: Ink can be found at 9 µm without a mesh
findings.text: On PHerc0841, a scroll the models never trained on, patches cut along the published surface prediction and inked with the standard 9 µm models find the human-labelled text at AUC 0.76, about 80 % of our full mesh pipeline on the same pixels. A method result on known text, not a discovery; whether it can steer a search is the next test.

findings.title: Test the search rule on the one real win
findings.text: Calibrated on clear known text, our row rule would have missed the PHerc. 0343 First Letters letters (faint, sparse, weak rows). A second line, reading-blind contrast, catches them with no new false alarms on 771 null winding-depths.

next: What the models respond to: the ablation on PHerc0841's letters (which layers, weave or brightness), before any try at synthetic training letters.
Geometry coverage: about a fifth of each fitted band repeats a sheet another winding covers; check it by eye, then count only unique area and look for the sheets in between.
Ink first with a point on every sheet: rank clusters of hot patches against the other face before any second whole-scroll sweep.
A better 8.64 µm model needs real human labels; collect published 8.64 µm text first.
Try the organisers' new neural sheet and fibre tracers (Sean Johnson's) to grow our meshes past their edges and to check them for jumps between sheets.
Choose the next scroll for a full search.

pipeline.title: How the pipeline works
pipeline.lede: From an X-ray scan of a rolled-up scroll to a decision about where to look next, in nine steps. Concepts only; each run page has the details.

stages.title: CT scan
stages.text: An X-ray volume of the rolled scroll. Every slice is a cross-section through all of its wound layers.
stages.alt: CT cross-section through PHerc. 0191: crushed and folded layers of papyrus

stages.title: Find the sheet
stages.text: Fit a spiral model of how the papyrus is wound to sheet tracks traced by the community and to predicted surfaces.
stages.alt: Diagram: a squashed spiral following the wound layers, with track points along it

stages.title: Snap
stages.text: Pull the fitted surface onto the papyrus surface a neural network predicted, so it sits on one real sheet.
stages.by: Erwin Nieuwlaar's snap, m7 surface prediction
stages.alt: Diagram: a dashed fitted line pulled down onto the solid predicted surface

stages.title: Flatten
stages.text: Unroll one winding into a flat sheet, so the papyrus, and any writing on it, appear at true size.
stages.alt: A flattened winding: the crossed fibres of the papyrus are visible

stages.title: Render
stages.text: Sample a thin stack of layers just inside and just outside the surface, like slicing the sheet into leaves.
stages.alt: Diagram: thin layers above and below the sheet surface

stages.title: Detect ink
stages.text: Several public ink models each mark where ink might be. Their maps are combined into one ensemble, for the writing side and for the back.
stages.by: ink_9um, dense_native, Hecate, Reader v2, d9v4C; ensemble after Erwin Nieuwlaar
stages.alt: Ensemble ink map of one flattened winding: mottled, no writing

stages.title: Rank
stages.text: The stroke score points to places where stroke-shaped marks show on the writing side but not on the back; a row score asks whether they line up in rows, as lines of text do.
stages.alt: Review crop: writing side, back and CT side by side

stages.title: Look
stages.text: We check flags and the top-ranked windings by eye against the CT and the back of the sheet, looking for rows of letter strokes. Cracks, voids, folds and zones that recur on neighbouring turns cause most false alarms.
stages.alt: Diagram: three panels labelled writing side, back and CT

stages.title: Gate
stages.text: Decide: go deeper here, move to the next band, or move to the next scroll. A new band or scroll starts again at step 2.
stages.alt: Diagram: a decision with three ways out: go deeper, next band, next scroll

control.title: Positive control
control.text: Known letters go through the same render, ink, rank and look steps: PHerc. 0343 (Erwin Nieuwlaar's First Letters segment, 8.64 µm), and PHerc0139 and PHerc0841 at 9.36 µm, the resolution we search. The letter rows have to light up there; if they did not, a blank result on our scroll would mean nothing. They do, as rows of strokes.
control.alt: Ensemble ink map of the PHerc. 0343 control: two rows of bright letter strokes

items.label: Home GPUs
items.text: The default for everything: it costs nothing extra and the data lives there.

items.label: Cloud GPUs
items.text: Short bursts next to the data, only when it is cost-effective, for example to get a fast answer on something promising.
